prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on a magic-wavelength lattice, and for its realisation as a many-atom frequency standard with fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened rather than changed the reasons. The central idea is Katori's magic-wavelength lattice: at a specific wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so many neutral atoms can be held in a Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. Ye's strontium work then showed that this scheme delivers stability and accuracy near 1e-18. These claims are credible because the atomic-structure inputs (dynamic polarizabilities, blackbody-radiation shifts, higher-order lattice shifts) can be calculated and measured independently, and they agree across laboratories and species. The consequences are physical observations, not only metrology: gravitational redshift resolved over a millimetre-scale sample and a concrete route to redefining the second. The credit divides into concept (Katori) and limiting performance (Ye), so a two-name prize needs no forced exclusions among the credited names. I would draft the citation around the lattice concept so that it stands apart from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still lineage: 2005 recognised laser precision spectroscopy and the frequency comb, 2012 recognised control of single quantum systems with ion clocks as a showcase, and a committee could read lattice clocks as a third prize in one line. The fundamental-physics results to date are null tests, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. Lemonde, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made real contributions that a two-name credit leaves outside, so the claim of a clean credit rests on the supplied record. Danielsson's argument that B009 is a new state of matter, while B049 is a gain in measurement quality, is a serious one that I have not refuted: it is a judgement about what counts as discovery, not a factual dispute. Finally, B009 has the broadest opening support, and my own specialist confidence in B049 may inflate my ranking.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B009 first as a new state of matter that is clearly attributable now, and says a mature metrology result such as B049 can wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a new phenomenon and a better measurement, and I will not claim that the clock is a new state of matter. My reply is that the many-atom magic-wavelength regime is a new physical scheme, one whose consequences, such as resolving the redshift across a millimetre, are observations that were not possible before. On waiting for the redefinition: the prize is for the invention and its demonstrated performance, and the redefinition is a decision of the metrology community that follows from that performance. If we make the prize conditional on it, we reward administrative timing. I would ask you to apply the same test to B009: if a settled mechanism is not required there, as you and Mehlig argue, then an unmade redefinition is not required here.

responses.point: Mehlig, now ranking B009 first, argues that the Nobel standard is a robust and reproduced discovery, not a complete explanation, and that the citation should be worded around the predicted flat bands and observed states, not the pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I agree with that standard and have said so. It cuts in both directions and it is why I do not rest my objection to B009 on the pairing mechanism alone. My reservations are two: the correlated phases are sensitive to twist-angle disorder and strain, which Olsson raised, and the theory credit has a documented precursor in Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto. Neither would stop me from supporting B009. If the committee wants a flat-band-and-observed-states citation with MacDonald, Bistritzer and Jarillo-Herrero, I can support that wording. I still judge that B049 is the less contested of the two on both attribution and maturity of understanding, and I take your point that it is the fallback if a stricter maturity bar is set.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B009 first on its testable prediction, imageable moire structure and lasting platform, but names disorder, strain, the Lopes dos Santos precursor and the open experimental credit as reasons the committee might wait, and lists B049 as a more mature fallback.
responses.response: Your candour about disorder and sample dependence matters to me, because it is the concern I can judge least from my own field and you can judge best. If the structural variation still changes which phases appear, then attributing the observed states to a single twist angle is less closed than the one-sentence summary suggests. I would put that to the supporters of B009. I also note that you name B049 as an alternative, so our disagreement is about timing, not about scientific quality. I would answer that two decades of independent confirmation and an understood error budget are the better basis for a prize that must withstand later developments.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved to B049 after the opening statements, lists the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main novelty risk and Lemonde and Ludlow as possible claimants, and asks whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: Pearce asked in round 1 whether I see any weakness in the distinction between the 2005 comb prize, the 2012 single-system prize and the lattice clock. I see one limit. The distinction holds for the physics, but it does not by itself settle the citation, since Ye's programme grew out of the comb tradition and a careless wording would reintroduce the overlap. So the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice and the many-atom regime explicitly and say nothing about frequency combs or ion control. On Lemonde and Ludlow, I think the committee can defend two names, but only if it states openly that other groups contributed. I do not think a fair third name can be chosen without weakening the concept-plus-performance logic.

responses.point: Johansson now prefers B012 with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, noting that the discovery chain is clear and replicated, but also that Cirac and Jaksch are left out and that the analogue-simulation payoff is not yet demonstrated.
responses.response: I see why B012 draws you: the Mott transition and the quantum gas microscope are real physics and replicated, and I keep it as my second alternative. But the credit problem you describe is serious. With four names for three places and Jaksch outside the list, the committee would have to choose between the proposal and the realisation in a way the clock case does not require. The 2001 and 2012 prizes are also close to this topic. I would be more comfortable with B012 if the committee could settle whether the theory name is Zoller or Cirac, and I would support it before I would support leaving the lattice clock for a third time.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, which depends heavily on how the citation is drafted.
Whether Lemonde, Ludlow or the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups have a claim strong enough to require a third name, in a case where I currently find a two-name credit defensible.
Whether the committee will accept a discovery standard under which a precision-measurement invention counts equally with a new phenomenon such as B009.
Whether B009's broad opening support should outweigh the open pairing mechanism, the sensitivity to disorder and the Lopes dos Santos precursor.
How far my specialist confidence in the atomic-structure details of B049 is raising my ranking relative to candidates I cannot assess in the same detail.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B049, B009 or B012 from my profile. My documented collaborators and contacts (Lindgren's Gothenburg group, L'Huillier and Lund colleagues, Keller's group at ETH, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) are not among the credited names for these candidates. I note a disciplinary closeness to the optical-clock field as a theorist in atomic physics, not a personal tie, and I treat it as a possible bias, as already stated in round 1. I have no connection to the Boulder or JILA environment that Kroll has disclosed, and my disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
